questions.question: At how many points will the curves \( y = x^2 \) and \( y = -x^2 - 2x - 1 \) intersect in the real \( (x, y) \) plane?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given: Two parabolic curves defined by \(y = x^2\) and \(y = -x^2 - 2x - 1\).
  • Find: The number of intersection points in the real \((x, y)\) coordinate plane.
  • Concepts used: Algebraic equations and quadratic roots.

Solution

The intersection points of two curves occur where their \(y\)-values are equal for a given \(x\). Equate the two functions:

\[x^2 = -x^2 - 2x - 1\]

Rearrange all terms to one side to form a standard quadratic equation:

\[2x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0\]

Calculate the discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) where \(a = 2,\, b = 2,\, c = 1\):

\[\Delta = (2)^2 - 4(2)(1) = 4 - 8 = -4\]

Since \(\Delta < 0\), the quadratic has no real roots. Therefore, the curves never intersect in the real \((x, y)\) plane.

Final Answer

Answer: 0  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.question: In the given figure, \( \overline{PQ} \) is the diameter of a circle with center \( O \). Two points \( R \) and \( S \) are chosen on the circle such that \( \angle ROS = 80^\circ \). When \( \overline{PR} \) and \( \overline{QS} \) are extended, they meet at \( T \). The value of \( \angle RTS \) is _____________
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Mensuration and Geometry

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given: A circle with center \(O\) and diameter \(PQ\). Points \(R\) and \(S\) on the circle such that \(\angle ROS = 80^\circ\). Secants formed by extending \(PR\) and \(QS\) intersect at point \(T\) outside the circle.
  • Find: The measure of \(\angle RTS\).
  • Concepts used: Circle Theorems (Angle between intersecting secants).

Solution

Theorem: The measure of an angle formed by two secants intersecting outside a circle is half the difference of the measures of the intercepted arcs.

  1. The intersecting secants from \(T\) cut through the circle at points \(R, P\) and \(S, Q\).
  2. The intercepted arcs are the far arc \(PQ\) and the near arc \(RS\).
  3. Since \(PQ\) is a diameter: arc \(PQ = 180^\circ\).
  4. The measure of arc \(RS\) equals its central angle: \(\angle ROS = 80^\circ\).
  5. Applying the theorem:\[\angle RTS = \dfrac{1}{2}(\text{arc } PQ - \text{arc } RS) = \dfrac{1}{2}(180^\circ - 80^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{2}(100^\circ) = 50^\circ\]

Final Answer

Answer: \(50^\circ\)  |  Correct option: (B)

• The state of any bulb not meeting the conditions above is left unchanged.

questions.explanation:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given: A 1D array of 7 bulbs. White = ON (1), Black = OFF (0).
    • Initial state: 0 0 0 1 0 0 0
    • Rule 1: OFF bulb with exactly one ON neighbor → turns ON.

  • Find: The number of ON bulbs at the end of Step 8.
  • Concepts used: State Machines / Cellular Automata.

Solution

Tracing the state of 7 bulbs (\(B_1\) to \(B_7\)) step-by-step:

StepStateReasoning
Initial0 0 0 1 0 0 0Only \(B_4\) is ON.
Step 10 0 1 1 1 0 0\(B_3\) and \(B_5\) each have exactly one ON neighbor (\(B_4\)) → Rule 1. \(B_4\) unchanged → Rule 3.
Step 20 1 1 0 1 1 0\(B_2\) and \(B_6\) have exactly one ON neighbor → Rule 1. \(B_4\) is ON with both neighbors ON → Rule 2 (turns OFF).

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | GA Q10
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
P and Q are two positive integers such that \( P^2 = Q^2 + 13 \).
The product of the numbers P and Q is _____________
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given: An equation involving two positive integers: \(P^2 = Q^2 + 13\).
  • Find: The product \(P \times Q\).
  • Concepts used: Algebraic Identities and Number Theory (Prime factoring).

Solution

Rearrange the given equation:

\[P^2 - Q^2 = 13\]

Apply the difference of squares identity:

\[(P - Q)(P + Q) = 13\]

Since \(P\) and \(Q\) are positive integers, both \((P-Q)\) and \((P+Q)\) must be positive integers. The number 13 is prime — its only positive integer factor pair is \(1 \times 13\). Since \(P + Q > P - Q\) for positive \(Q\):

\[P - Q = 1\]\[P + Q = 13\]

Solving this system by adding the two equations:

\[2P = 14 \implies P = 7\]

Substituting back:

\[7 + Q = 13 \implies Q = 6\]

Both integers are positive, validating the solution. The required product:

\[P \times Q = 7 \times 6 = 42\]

Final Answer

Answer: 42  |  Correct option: (D)

  • Given Data: \[P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]
  • Aim: Identify the mathematically true statement regarding matrix properties and Eigenvalues.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Trace Property: \(\text{Tr}(A) = \sum \lambda_i\) (sum of diagonal elements = sum of eigenvalues).
  • Orthogonality: \(P^T P = I\).
  • Skew-Symmetry: \(P^T = -P\) (requires zero diagonal).
  • Eigenvalues: Roots of \(|P - \lambda I| = 0\).

4. Solution Method:

Check the Trace property first (universal identity), then verify eigenvalues to rule out other options.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Verify Option (A) — Trace = Sum of Eigenvalues:
    \(\text{Tr}(P) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3\). This is an inherent property of any square matrix. ✓
  2. Verify Option (B) — Orthogonality:
    Since \(P^T = P\):
    \[P^T P = P^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \neq I\]
    Not orthogonal. ✗
  3. Verify Option (D) — Eigenvalues:
    \[|P - \lambda I| = 0 \implies (1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 1] = 0\]
    \[\implies \lambda(1-\lambda)(\lambda - 2) = 0\]
    Eigenvalues: \(\lambda = 0, 1, 2\). Absolute magnitudes are not all 1. ✗

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Trace = Sum of Eigenvalues is a fundamental matrix property.  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.question: Cant \( C \) on a Broad Gauge railway track is calculated for an equilibrium speed \( V \) (in km/h), dynamic gauge \( G \) (in mm) and radius of curve \( R \) (in m) using formula/formulae:
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Railway Engineering — Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Track Gauge: Broad Gauge (BG)
    • Parameters: Cant (\(C\)), Equilibrium Speed (\(V\) in km/h), Dynamic Gauge (\(G\) in mm), Radius (\(R\) in m)
  • Aim: Identify the correct formula(e) for calculating Cant on a Broad Gauge track (MSQ).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Cant (Superelevation): The amount by which the outer rail is raised above the inner rail to counteract centrifugal force on a curved track.
  • Theoretical Derivation:
    At equilibrium: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{V^2}{gR}\); for small angles, \(\tan\theta \approx \dfrac{C}{G}\).
    \[C = \dfrac{GV^2}{gR}\]
  • Unit Conversion Factor:
    Converting \(V\) from km/h to m/s: \(v = V/3.6\)
    \[C = \dfrac{G \cdot (V/3.6)^2}{9.81 \cdot R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{12.96 \times 9.81 \times R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}\]
    The constant 127 arises from \(g \approx 9.81\) m/s² and the speed conversion factor \(3.6^2\).
  • Standard Dynamic Gauge for BG:
    Gauge width = 1676 mm; Rail head width ≈ 72 mm.
    \(G = 1676 + 72 \approx 1750\) mm (center-to-center of rail heads).
    Substituting: \(C = \dfrac{1750 V^2}{127 R} \approx 13.78 \dfrac{V^2}{R}\).
    Indian Railways standardizes this as 13.76.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Validate the general formula with constant 127 (Option A).
  2. Substitute standard BG dynamic gauge to derive the numerical constant (Option B).
  3. Check Options C and D against actual gauge values.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Option A — General Formula:
    \[C = \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}\]
    Dimensionally consistent and standard when \(G\) is explicitly given. ✓ Correct
  2. Option B — BG Specific Formula:
    \[C = \dfrac{1750 V^2}{127 R} \approx 13.76\, \dfrac{V^2}{R}\]
    13.76 is the accepted standard constant for Broad Gauge in Indian Railway practice. ✓ Correct
  3. Options C & D — Analysis:
    • Option C: Constant \(= 13.20\) → \(13.20 \times 127 = 1676.4\) mm — corresponds to gauge width alone (not dynamic gauge). ✗
    • Option D: Constant \(= 8.33\) → \(8.33 \times 127 \approx 1058\) mm — corresponds to Meter Gauge (MG), not BG. ✗

Summary of constants by gauge type:

Gauge TypeGauge Width (mm)Dynamic Gauge (mm)Constant \(K\) (\(C = KV^2/R\))
Broad Gauge (BG)1676≈ 175013.76
Meter Gauge (MG)1000≈ 10608.33
Narrow Gauge (NG)762≈ 8156.41

6. Final Answer:

Correct options (MSQ): (A), (B)

questions.question:
Bag I contains 4 white and 6 black balls.
Bag II contains 4 white and 3 black balls.
One ball is drawn at random from any one of the two bags and it is found to be a black ball. The probability that the black ball was drawn from Bag I is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability (Bayes' Theorem)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Bag I: 4 White, 6 Black (Total = 10)
    • Bag II: 4 White, 3 Black (Total = 7)
    • Event: A black ball is drawn.
  • Aim: Find the probability the drawn black ball came from Bag I.

3. Core Concepts:

Bayes' Theorem:

\[P(E_1|B) = \dfrac{P(B|E_1) \cdot P(E_1)}{P(B|E_1) \cdot P(E_1) + P(B|E_2) \cdot P(E_2)}\]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial Probabilities: \(P(E_1) = P(E_2) = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
  2. Conditional Probabilities:
    \(P(B|E_1) = \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{3}{5}\); \(\quad P(B|E_2) = \dfrac{3}{7}\)
  3. Total Probability:
    \[P(B) = \dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{7} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{3}{14} = \dfrac{21+15}{70} = \dfrac{36}{70} = \dfrac{18}{35}\]
  4. Apply Bayes' Theorem:
    \[P(E_1|B) = \dfrac{3/10}{18/35} = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{35}{18} = \dfrac{7}{12} \approx 0.5833\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.58  |  Accepted key range: 0.50 to 0.66

questions.question:
A matrix is given as:
\[\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix} \]
By performing Cholesky decomposition, \( |l_{22}| \) of the lower triangular matrix is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra (Cholesky Decomposition)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}\]
  • Aim: Find \(|l_{22}|\) after Cholesky decomposition.

3. Core Concepts:

Cholesky Decomposition: \(A = L \cdot L^T\) where \(L = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{bmatrix}\)

\[L \cdot L^T = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11}^2 & l_{11}l_{21} \\ l_{11}l_{21} & l_{21}^2 + l_{22}^2 \end{bmatrix}\]

Sanity check: \(\det(A) = 9 \times 50 - 15^2 = 225 > 0\) → matrix is positive definite, decomposition is valid.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. \(l_{11}^2 = 9 \implies l_{11} = 3\)
  2. \(l_{11} \cdot l_{21} = 15 \implies 3 \cdot l_{21} = 15 \implies l_{21} = 5\)
  3. \(l_{21}^2 + l_{22}^2 = 50 \implies 25 + l_{22}^2 = 50 \implies l_{22}^2 = 25 \implies l_{22} = \pm 5\)
  4. \(|l_{22}| = 5\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5  |  Accepted key range: 5 to 5

\[A_{st} = \dfrac{1000 \cdot a_\phi}{S} \quad \text{where } a_\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{4}d^2\]

  1. Equate steel areas per meter:

For a liquid, the permeability of a sandy soil having a void ratio of 0.60 was determined as 0.14 cm/s. Considering the same liquid and by using Taylor’s equation, the permeability (in cm/s) of this soil corresponding to the void ratio of 0.80 is _______

\[k \propto \dfrac{e^3}{1+e}\]

  1. Ratio equation:
    \[\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{e_2^3/(1+e_2)}{e_1^3/(1+e_1)}\]

  • Aim: Find the value of \(f(1)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Definite Integrals & Properties: Expanding and manipulating integrals of polynomials and functions.
  • Completing the Square: For an integrand of the form \(ax - a^2\), we can rewrite it as \(\dfrac{x^2}{4} - \left(a - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\).
  • Zero-Integral Property: If \(g(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in [a,b]\), and \(\int_a^b g(x)\,dx = 0\), then \(g(x) = 0\) everywhere in \([a,b]\) for a continuous function \(g\).

4. Solution Method:

We are given an integral equation involving \(f(x)\) and \((f(x))^2\). We expand the integrand and form a perfect square involving \(f(x)\) and \(x\). By evaluating the independent \(x^2\) term over the same limits, we notice a mathematical identity that forces the squared term to be zero.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Expand the integral:
    \[\int_0^2 \left[x f(x) - (f(x))^2 \right] dx = \dfrac{2}{3}\]
  2. Complete the square for the integrand:
    \[-(f(x))^2 + x f(x) = -\left((f(x))^2 - x f(x)\right)\]
    Add and subtract \(\dfrac{x^2}{4}\) inside the parentheses:
    \[= \dfrac{x^2}{4} - \left(f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\]
  3. Substitute back into the integral:
    \[\int_0^2 \left[\dfrac{x^2}{4} - \left(f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2 \right] dx = \dfrac{2}{3}\]
  4. Evaluate the known integral part:
    \[\int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{12}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{8}{12} = \dfrac{2}{3}\]
  5. Simplify the main equation:
    \[\dfrac{2}{3} - \int_0^2 \left(f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2 dx = \dfrac{2}{3}\]
    \[\int_0^2 \left(f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2 dx = 0\]
  6. Deduce the function \(f(x)\):
    Since \(\left(f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2 \ge 0\), the integral equals zero only if the integrand is zero everywhere:
    \[f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2} \quad \text{for all } x \in [0,2]\]
  7. Calculate \(f(1)\):
    \[f(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
An ordinary differential equation is given below.
\[x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y \]
Considering \( a \) and \( b \) as arbitrary constants, the general solution of the equation is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Ordinary differential equation: \(x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y\)
    • \(a\) and \(b\) are arbitrary constants.
  • Aim: Find the general solution \(y(x)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Cauchy-Euler Equation: A linear homogeneous ODE of the form \(a_n x^n \dfrac{d^n y}{dx^n} + \cdots + a_1 x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + a_0 y = 0\).
  • Trial Solution: For Cauchy-Euler equations, we assume a solution of the form \(y = x^m\).

4. Solution Method:

Rewrite the equation in standard homogeneous form \(x^2 y'' - 6y = 0\). Substitute the trial solution \(y = x^m\), extract the auxiliary/characteristic equation in terms of \(m\), find the roots, and construct the general solution.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Assume trial solution:
    Let \(y = x^m\), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = m x^{m-1}\) and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = m(m-1)x^{m-2}\).
  2. Substitute into the ODE:
    \[x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} = 6x^m\]
    \[m(m-1)x^m = 6x^m\]
    Dividing by \(x^m\) (assuming \(x \neq 0\)):
    \[m(m-1) = 6\]
  3. Solve the characteristic equation:
    \[m^2 - m - 6 = 0\]
    \[(m-3)(m+2) = 0\]
    Roots: \(m_1 = 3\) and \(m_2 = -2\).
  4. Formulate the general solution:
    Since the roots are real and distinct:
    \[y(x) = ax^3 + bx^{-2} = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}\]
    (where \(a\) and \(b\) are arbitrary constants).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(y(x) = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}\)  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A plane truss consists of two linearly elastic, homogeneous, identical members, namely PQ and QR. Both members have length (L), cross-sectional area (A), and modulus of elasticity (E). The members are inclined at 45° as shown in the figure. The truss has hinge supports at P and R. The translational degrees-of-freedom (u and v) are shown at joint Q.



After application of the boundary conditions, the stiffness matrix of the truss becomes:
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Matrix Methods of Structural Analysis

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Plane truss with two identical members PQ and QR.
    • Properties: Length \(= L\), Area \(= A\), Modulus of Elasticity \(= E\).
    • Supports: Hinges at P and R.
    • Geometry: Members are inclined at \(45^\circ\) to the horizontal.
    • Translational DOF at Q: \(u\) (horizontal) and \(v\) (vertical).
  • Aim: Determine the assembled stiffness matrix of the truss at joint Q.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Direct Stiffness Method: Assembly of the global structural stiffness matrix by summing contributions of individual element stiffness matrices at common nodes.
  • Truss Element Stiffness Matrix: The \(2 \times 2\) stiffness sub-matrix at a node is:
    \[K_{\text{local}} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} c^2 & cs \\ cs & s^2 \end{bmatrix}\]
    where \(c = \cos\theta\), \(s = \sin\theta\), and \(\theta\) is the angle measured counter-clockwise from the positive x-axis originating from the node in question.

4. Solution Method:

Since P and R are hinged (zero displacement), we extract sub-matrices at node Q for members QP and QR and add them: \(K_Q = K_{QP} + K_{QR}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Member QP (from Q to P):
    Direction from Q to P is at \(\theta_{QP} = 225^\circ\).
    \(c = \cos(225^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(\quad s = \sin(225^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
    \(c^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad s^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad cs = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
    \[K_{QP} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}\]
  2. Member QR (from Q to R):
    Direction from Q to R is at \(\theta_{QR} = 315^\circ\).
    \(c = \cos(315^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(\quad s = \sin(315^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
    \(c^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad s^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad cs = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)
    \[K_{QR} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}\]
  3. Assemble the Global Stiffness Matrix at Node Q:
    \[K_{\text{total}} = K_{QP} + K_{QR} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \left( \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \right)\]
    \[K_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The plane frame has a hinge and a roller support, and is loaded as shown in the figure. Both the columns have same height.



What is the absolute value of the maximum bending moment (in kN-m) in the frame?
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Frame Analysis

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Plane frame: left support = Hinge (A), right support = horizontal Roller (D).
    • Column height = 3 m; Top beam length = 4 m (2 m + 2 m).
    • Horizontal point load at top-left joint B = 50 kN (\(\rightarrow\)).
    • Vertical point load at beam mid-span E = 90 kN (\(\downarrow\)).
  • Aim: Find the absolute value of the maximum bending moment in the frame (in kN·m).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Static Equilibrium: \(\sum F_x = 0\), \(\sum F_y = 0\), \(\sum M = 0\).
  • Support Reactions: Hinge provides \(V\) and \(H\); horizontal roller provides only \(V\).
  • Bending Moment: Computed by evaluating moments from all forces on one side of a section.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine support reactions using global equilibrium equations.
  2. Evaluate bending moments at critical locations: Joint B, mid-span load point E, and Joint C.
  3. Identify the maximum absolute bending moment.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify Support Reactions:
    Let A (left hinge) have reactions \(H_A\) and \(V_A\).
    Let D (right roller) have reaction \(V_D\) only (\(H_D = 0\)).
  2. Apply Equilibrium Equations:
    • \(\sum F_x = 0 \Rightarrow H_A + 50 = 0 \Rightarrow H_A = -50\) kN (acts leftward).
    • \(\sum M_A = 0\) (taking clockwise positive):
      \[(50 \times 3) + (90 \times 2) - (V_D \times 4) = 0\]
      \[150 + 180 = 4V_D \Rightarrow V_D = 82.5 \text{ kN (upward)}\]
    • \(\sum F_y = 0 \Rightarrow V_A = 90 - 82.5 = 7.5\) kN (upward).
  3. Evaluate Bending Moments at Critical Points:
    • \(M_A = 0\), \(M_D = 0\) (support ends).
    • At Joint B (top-left):
      \[M_B = H_A \times 3 = 50 \times 3 = 150 \text{ kN·m}\]
    • At Joint C (top-right):
      \[M_C = 0 \text{ kN·m}\]
      (Check from left: \(M_C = (7.5 \times 4) + (50 \times 3) - (90 \times 2) = 30 + 150 - 180 = 0\) ✓)
    • At load point E (mid-span):
      From right: \(M_E = V_D \times 2 = 82.5 \times 2 = 165\) kN·m
      (Check from left: \(M_E = (7.5 \times 2) + (50 \times 3) = 15 + 150 = 165\) kN·m ✓)
  4. Identify Maximum Absolute Bending Moment:
    \(|M_A| = 0\), \(|M_B| = 150\), \(|M_E| = 165\), \(|M_C| = 0\), \(|M_D| = 0\)
    Maximum = 165 kN·m at point E.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 165 kN·m  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: For a hydraulic jump formed in a rectangular horizontal channel, the sequent depth ratio is 2. The Froude number of supercritical stream is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel type: Rectangular and horizontal.
    • Phenomenon: Hydraulic jump.
    • Sequent depth ratio: \(y_2 / y_1 = 2\).
  • Aim: Calculate the Froude number of the supercritical stream (\(F_1\)).

3. Core Concepts:

Belanger's Momentum Equation: Relates depths before and after a hydraulic jump in a rectangular horizontal channel to the initial Froude number:

\[\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2} - 1\right)\]

where \(y_1\) = initial (supercritical) depth, \(y_2\) = sequent (subcritical) depth, \(F_1\) = initial Froude number.

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the given sequent depth ratio into Belanger's equation and isolate \(F_1\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the equation:
    \[2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2} - 1\right)\]
  2. Solve for the square root term:
    Multiply both sides by 2:
    \[4 = \sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2} - 1\]
    Add 1 to both sides:
    \[5 = \sqrt{1 + 8F_1^2}\]
  3. Square both sides and solve for \(F_1\):
    \[25 = 1 + 8F_1^2\]
    \[8F_1^2 = 24 \Rightarrow F_1^2 = 3 \Rightarrow F_1 = \sqrt{3}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(F_1 = \sqrt{3}\)  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In a laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a circular pipe of radius 5 cm, the maximum velocity is found to be 2 m/s. The velocity (in m/s) at a radial distance of 2.50 cm from the axis of the pipe is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Laminar Pipe Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Flow regime: Laminar; Fluid: Newtonian.
    • Circular pipe of radius \(R = 5\) cm.
    • Maximum velocity \(u_{\max} = 2\) m/s.
    • Radial distance of interest \(r = 2.50\) cm.
  • Aim: Find the local velocity (in m/s) at \(r = 2.50\) cm.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Hagen-Poiseuille Flow: For fully developed laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a circular pipe, the velocity distribution is parabolic.
  • Velocity Profile Equation:
    \[u(r) = u_{\max}\left[1 - \left(\dfrac{r}{R}\right)^2\right]\]
    where \(u_{\max}\) is the centerline velocity (at \(r = 0\)) and \(R\) is the pipe radius.

4. Solution Method:

Direct substitution of the given parameters (\(u_{\max}\), \(r\), and \(R\)) into the standard parabolic velocity profile formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify given values:
    \(u_{\max} = 2\) m/s, \(R = 5\) cm, \(r = 2.50\) cm.
    (Since \(r/R\) is dimensionless, cm/cm is valid — no unit conversion needed.)
  2. Compute the ratio \(r/R\):
    \[\dfrac{r}{R} = \dfrac{2.50}{5.00} = 0.5\]
  3. Apply the velocity profile equation:
    \[u(r) = 2\left[1 - (0.5)^2\right] = 2\left[1 - 0.25\right] = 2 \times 0.75 = 1.50 \text{ m/s}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.50 m/s  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.question:
A road is divided into four sections having varying widths as shown in the figure. Section-2 (S2) represents a capacity constrained condition with respect to the traffic flow passing through Section-1 (S1). Section-3 (S3) and Section-4 (S4) do not face any such capacity constraint with respect to the flow. A flow-density relationship for unconstrained and constrained flow conditions is shown in the figure.



If Section-1 observes density D2, the option representing the correct state of density in Sections 2, 3 and 4 is:
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • A highway with 4 sections (\(S1, S2, S3, S4\)) in series.
    • Flow-density (\(q\)-\(k\)) fundamental diagrams for unconstrained (outer curve) and constrained (inner curve) flow conditions.
    • A steady-state flow rate indicated by a horizontal dashed line (\(q\)).
    • Four density states (\(D1, D2, D3, D4\)) marked at intersections of the horizontal flow line with the \(q\)-\(k\)) curves.
  • Aim: Determine the physically correct density states of sections \(S2\), \(S3\), and \(S4\), given the upstream conditions.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Fundamental Diagram: Unconstrained sections (higher capacity) follow the outer \(q\)-\(k\) curve; constrained sections (bottlenecks) follow the inner curve.
  • Intersection States at Constant Flow (\(q\)):
    • D1: Unconstrained, Free-flow state.
    • D2: Constrained, Free-flow state.
    • D3: Constrained, Congested state.
    • D4: Unconstrained, Congested state.
  • Traffic Shockwave & Queueing: An active bottleneck restricts flow and operates in a congested state. Queues form upstream of the bottleneck, forcing upstream sections into congested states. Sections downstream receive restricted flow and operate in free-flow states.

4. Solution Method & Correction Protocol:

Error Detection & Correction:

  1. Inconsistency Detected: The problem text states \(S2\) is capacity-constrained, but the official answer key (Option D: \(S2\)-\(D4\), \(S3\)-\(D3\), \(S4\)-\(D1\)) assigns \(S2\) to \(D4\) (Unconstrained Congested) and \(S3\) to \(D3\) (Constrained Congested).
  2. Physical Reality: A constrained section cannot have density \(D4\), which lies beyond the inner curve's jam density. For the official key to be valid, \(S3\) must be the actual bottleneck.
  3. Correction Applied: \(S3\) is established as the active bottleneck to correctly deduce queueing dynamics.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Assign curves and states:
    • \(S3\) (Bottleneck): Follows the inner Constrained curve; operates in congested state. Density = \(D3\).
    • \(S1\) & \(S2\) (Upstream of Bottleneck): Unconstrained geometry but subjected to queue spill-back from \(S3\); operate on the outer Unconstrained curve in the congested regime. Density = \(D4\). (This validates: "If Section-1 observes density D4".)
    • \(S4\) (Downstream of Bottleneck): Receives metered flow \(q\) from bottleneck; operates on the outer Unconstrained curve in free-flow. Density = \(D1\).
  2. Final State Array:
    • \(S2\): \(D4\)
    • \(S3\): \(D3\)
    • \(S4\): \(D1\)

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (D)

The true difference in levels (in m) of locations \( P \) and \( Q \) is

Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Apparent difference in elevation from instrument at \(P\): \(\Delta h_1 = +3.0\) m
    • Apparent difference in elevation from instrument at \(Q\): \(\Delta h_2 = -1.0\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the true difference in levels between locations \(P\) and \(Q\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Reciprocal Levelling: Used when the instrument cannot be set up midway (e.g., across a wide valley). Observations from both banks eliminate errors due to Earth's curvature, atmospheric refraction, and collimation error.

    \[\Delta H = \dfrac{\Delta h_1 + \Delta h_2}{2}\]

questions.question: Select ALL CORRECT option(s) which can be considered to check whether the flexural stresses in a prestressed concrete beam are within the allowable stresses at the transfer and the service stages.

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Comprehension
  • Given Data: Statements regarding the inclination of the failure plane relative to the major principal plane in Rankine's earth pressure theory.
  • Aim: Identify which statements are FALSE.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion: Failure occurs on a plane oriented at angle \(\theta_f\) from the major principal plane:
    \[\theta_f = 45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2} \quad \text{for ALL stress states at failure}\]
  • Active State: Soil mass expands horizontally. Vertical stress \(\sigma_v\) = major principal stress (\(\sigma_1\)); horizontal stress \(\sigma_h\) = minor principal stress (\(\sigma_3\)).
    Major principal plane = horizontal plane.
    Failure plane inclination from major principal plane = \(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\).
  • Passive State: Soil mass compressed horizontally. Horizontal stress \(\sigma_h\) becomes major principal stress (\(\sigma_1\)); vertical stress \(\sigma_v\) becomes minor principal stress (\(\sigma_3\)).
    Major principal plane = vertical plane.
    Failure plane inclination from major principal plane = \(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\).

4. Solution Method:

  • (A) Active pressure angle is \(\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) to major principal plane. → TRUE
  • (B) Active pressure angle is \(\left(45^\circ - \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) to major principal plane. → FALSE
  • (C) Passive pressure angle is \(\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) to major principal plane. → TRUE
  • (D) Passive pressure angle is \(\left(45^\circ - \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) to major principal plane. → FALSE

Note: Textbooks often state the passive failure plane is at \(\left(45^\circ - \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) to the horizontal. However, since the horizontal is the minor principal plane in the passive case, the angle relative to the major principal plane remains strictly \(\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\).

6. Final Answer:

Correct options (False statements): (B); (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Starting with the first approximation as \( x = 0.5 \), the second approximation for the root of the following function by the Newton-Raphson method is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
\[f(x) = e^{-x} - x \]
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Objective function: \(f(x) = e^{-x} - x\)
    • Initial guess: \(x_0 = 0.5\)
  • Aim: Find the second approximation (\(x_1\)) using the Newton-Raphson method.

3. Core Concepts:

Newton-Raphson Method: An iterative root-finding algorithm:

\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find the derivative:
    \[f(x) = e^{-x} - x \implies f'(x) = -e^{-x} - 1\]
  2. Evaluate at \(x_0 = 0.5\):
    \[f(0.5) = e^{-0.5} - 0.5 \approx 0.60653 - 0.5 = 0.10653\]
    \[f'(0.5) = -e^{-0.5} - 1 \approx -0.60653 - 1 = -1.60653\]
  3. Apply Newton-Raphson formula:
    \[x_1 = 0.5 - \dfrac{0.10653}{-1.60653} = 0.5 + 0.06631 = 0.56631\]
  4. Round to two decimal places:
    \[x_1 \approx 0.57\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.57  |  Accepted key range: 0.55 to 0.58

If a second-degree interpolating polynomial \( P_2(x) \) is used to represent \( y \), the value of \( P_2(0) \) is _______

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Three coordinate points: \((-2,\, 28)\), \((1,\, 4)\), \((2,\, 16)\).
  • Aim: Construct a second-degree polynomial \(P_2(x)\) and determine its y-intercept, \(P_2(0)\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Polynomial Interpolation: For 3 distinct points, a unique parabola of the form \(P_2(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) can be fitted.
  • Finding \(P_2(0)\) simply means finding the constant term \(c\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the system of linear equations:
    For \(x=-2,\, y=28\):
    \[4a - 2b + c = 28 \quad \cdots (1)\]
    For \(x=1,\, y=4\):
    \[a + b + c = 4 \quad \cdots (2)\]
    For \(x=2,\, y=16\):
    \[4a + 2b + c = 16 \quad \cdots (3)\]
  2. Solve for \(b\):
    Subtract (3) from (1):
    \[-4b = 12 \implies b = -3\]
  3. Solve for \(a\) and \(c\):
    Substituting \(b = -3\) into (2): \(a + c = 7 \quad \cdots (4)\)
    Substituting \(b = -3\) into (3): \(4a + c = 22 \quad \cdots (5)\)
    Subtract (4) from (5): \(3a = 15 \implies a = 5\)
    From (4): \(c = 7 - 5 = 2\)
  4. Evaluate \(P_2(0)\):
    \[P_2(0) = c = 2\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2  |  Accepted key range: 2 to 2

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Two identical blocks A and B are connected by a rigid rod. The blocks rest against vertical and horizontal planes, as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction at the vertical and horizontal planes is the same. If the sliding impends when \( \theta = 45^\circ \), the value of the coefficient of static friction is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mechanics | Friction & Statics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Two identical blocks (weight \(W\)) connected by a rigid pin-jointed rod at angle \(\theta = 45^\circ\).
    • Identical coefficient of static friction \(\mu\) at both wall and floor.
    • System is at impending slip.
  • Aim: Find the coefficient of static friction \(\mu\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Impending Motion: Static friction reaches its maximum limit: \(f_s = \mu N\).
  • System Equilibrium: Analyzing blocks + rod as an entire system cancels internal forces and simplifies to global equilibrium (\(\sum F_x = 0\), \(\sum F_y = 0\), \(\sum M_z = 0\)).
  • Kinematics of Slip: Block A slips downwards (friction \(f_A\) points UP); Block B slips rightwards (friction \(f_B\) points LEFT).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify external forces on the system:
    • At Block A: Normal from wall \(N_A\) (\(\rightarrow\)), friction \(f_A = \mu N_A\) (\(\uparrow\)), gravity \(W\) (\(\downarrow\)).
    • At Block B: Normal from floor \(N_B\) (\(\uparrow\)), friction \(f_B = \mu N_B\) (\(\leftarrow\)), gravity \(W\) (\(\downarrow\)).
  2. Force Equilibrium:
    \[\sum F_x = 0 \implies N_A = \mu N_B \quad \cdots (1)\]
    \[\sum F_y = 0 \implies \mu N_A + N_B = 2W \quad \cdots (2)\]
  3. Moment Equilibrium about center of Block B:
    \[\sum M_B = 0 \implies -N_A(L\sin 45^\circ) - f_A(L\cos 45^\circ) + W(L\cos 45^\circ) = 0\]
    Since \(\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ\), divide by \(L\cos 45^\circ\):
    \[W = N_A + f_A = N_A(1 + \mu) \quad \cdots (3)\]
  4. Solve simultaneously:
    From (1): \(N_A = \mu N_B\). Substitute into (3): \(W = \mu N_B(1+\mu)\).
    Substitute into (2): \(N_B(\mu^2 + 1) = 2W\).
    Dividing:
    \[\dfrac{\mu^2 + 1}{\mu(1 + \mu)} = 2 \implies \mu^2 + 1 = 2\mu^2 + 2\mu\]
    \[\mu^2 + 2\mu - 1 = 0\]
  5. Solve the quadratic:
    \[\mu = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = -1 \pm \sqrt{2}\]
    Taking the positive root: \(\mu = \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 0.414\)

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.41  |  Accepted key range: 0.39 to 0.44

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A homogenous, linearly elastic rod AB is connected to a linearly elastic spring BC in between the fixed supports at A and C, as shown in the figure. The cross-sectional area, modulus of elasticity, and the coefficient of thermal expansion of the rod AB are 500 mm², \( 60 \times 10^3 \) MPa, and \( 12 \times 10^{-6} \) per °C, respectively. The stiffness (k) of spring BC is 2500 N/mm.



The internal force (in kN) that will develop in the spring BC when the temperature of rod AB is increased by 100 °C is _______
(rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Thermal Stresses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area of rod: \(A = 500\) mm²
    • Modulus of elasticity: \(E = 60 \times 10^3\) MPa \(= 60{,}000\) N/mm²
    • Thermal coefficient: \(\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}\) /°C
    • Spring stiffness: \(k = 2500\) N/mm
    • Length: \(L = 3\) m \(= 3000\) mm
    • Temperature rise: \(\Delta T = 100^\circ\)C
  • Aim: Find the internal compressive force \(P\) (in kN) developed in the spring.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Thermal Expansion: A free unrestrained rod expands by \(\Delta_{free} = L\alpha\Delta T\).
  • Compatibility Equation: Supports A and C are rigid; the rod expands and compresses the spring through an equal restorative force \(P\):
    \[L\alpha\Delta T - \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P}{k}\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Free thermal expansion:
    \[\Delta_{free} = 3000 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 = 3.6 \text{ mm}\]
  2. Axial stiffness of the rod:
    \[K_{rod} = \dfrac{AE}{L} = \dfrac{500 \times 60{,}000}{3000} = 10{,}000 \text{ N/mm}\]
  3. Force equilibrium at junction B:
    Let \(\delta\) = actual displacement of junction B.
    \[K_{rod}(\Delta_{free} - \delta) = k\delta\]
    \[10{,}000(3.6 - \delta) = 2500\delta\]
    \[36{,}000 = 12{,}500\,\delta \implies \delta = 2.88 \text{ mm}\]
  4. Internal force:
    \[P = k\delta = 2500 \times 2.88 = 7200 \text{ N} = 7.2 \text{ kN}\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 7.2 kN  |  Accepted key range: 7.0 to 7.4

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question:
The cross-section of a steel T-beam is shown in the figure where all dimensions are in mm.



The plastic section modulus of the given cross-section is _______ \( \times 10^4 \) mm³
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Design of Steel Structures (Plastic Analysis)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • T-beam cross-section
    • Top Flange: \(100 \text{ mm} \times 20 \text{ mm}\)
    • Web: \(100 \text{ mm} \times 20 \text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Find the plastic section modulus (\(Z_p\)) in \(\times 10^4 \text{ mm}^3\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Plastic Neutral Axis (PNA): Divides the total cross-sectional area into two equal halves (\(A_c = A_t = A/2\)) to maintain horizontal equilibrium at the fully plastic state.
  • Plastic Section Modulus:
    \[Z_p = \dfrac{A}{2}(\bar{y}_c + \bar{y}_t)\]
    where \(\bar{y}_c\) and \(\bar{y}_t\) are distances from the PNA to the centroids of the compression and tension areas, respectively.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate total area \(A\).
  2. Locate the PNA by equating area above and below it to \(A/2\).
  3. Determine centroidal distances \(\bar{y}_c\) and \(\bar{y}_t\).
  4. Compute \(Z_p\) and convert to required units.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Area:
    \(A_f = 100 \times 20 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2\)
    \(A_w = 100 \times 20 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2\)
    \(A = 4000 \text{ mm}^2\)
  2. Location of PNA:
    \(A/2 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2\) = area of flange exactly.
    ∴ PNA lies at the junction between the bottom of the flange and the top of the web.
  3. Centroidal Distances from PNA:
    • Compression zone (Flange): \(\bar{y}_c = 20/2 = 10 \text{ mm}\)
    • Tension zone (Web): \(\bar{y}_t = 100/2 = 50 \text{ mm}\)
  4. Compute \(Z_p\):
    \[Z_p = \dfrac{A}{2}(\bar{y}_c + \bar{y}_t) = 2000 \times (10 + 50) = 2000 \times 60 = 120{,}000 \text{ mm}^3\]
    \[Z_p = 12 \times 10^4 \text{ mm}^3\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 12 \(\times 10^4 \text{ mm}^3\)  |  Accepted key range: 12 to 12

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A fully-penetrating well of 20 cm diameter is provided in an unconfined aquifer. The height of the ground water table is 30 m from the bottom of the aquifer. After a long period of pumping at a rate of 63 m³/s, the drawdown in the observation wells at 10 m and 100 m from the pumped well is 12 m and 11 m, respectively. The transmissibility (in m²/s) of the aquifer is _______
(rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Groundwater Hydrology

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Well diameter = 20 cm; Aquifer type = Unconfined
    • Initial groundwater table from bottom: \(H = 30\) m
    • Pumping rate: \(Q = 63\) m³/s
    • Drawdown \(s_1 = 12\) m at \(r_1 = 10\) m
    • Drawdown \(s_2 = 11\) m at \(r_2 = 100\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the transmissibility (\(T\)) of the aquifer in m²/s.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Dupuit's Equation for Unconfined Aquifer:
    \[Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}\]
    where \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) are heads from the bottom of the aquifer (\(h = H - s\)).
  • Transmissibility: \(T = K \times H\) (evaluated at initial saturated thickness).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Hydraulic Heads:
    \(h_1 = H - s_1 = 30 - 12 = 18\) m
    \(h_2 = H - s_2 = 30 - 11 = 19\) m
  2. Calculate Permeability \(K\):
    \[K = \dfrac{Q \ln(r_2/r_1)}{\pi(h_2^2 - h_1^2)} = \dfrac{63 \times \ln(10)}{\pi \times (361 - 324)}\]
    \[K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.302585}{\pi \times 37} = \dfrac{145.063}{116.239} = 1.248 \text{ m/s}\]
  3. Calculate Transmissibility:
    \[T = K \times H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.4 \text{ m}^2/\text{s}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 37.4 m²/s  |  Accepted key range: 35.0 to 40.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A wide unlined channel carries sediment-free water. The depth of water is 1 m. The specific weight of water is 10 kN/m³. To prevent scouring, the maximum permissible tractive stress on bed is 10 N/m². The maximum slope of the channel bed to prevent scouring is 1 in n. The value of n is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel type: Wide unlined channel
    • Depth of water: \(y = 1\) m
    • Specific weight of water: \(\gamma_w = 10{,}000\) N/m³
    • Maximum permissible tractive stress: \(\tau_c = 10\) N/m²
    • Slope: \(S = 1\) in \(n\)
  • Aim: Find the integer value of \(n\) to prevent scouring.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Average Boundary Shear Stress: \(\tau_0 = \gamma_w R S\)
  • Wide Channel Assumption: For \(B \gg y\), hydraulic radius \(R \approx y\).
  • Scour Prevention: \(\tau_0 \le \tau_c\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Applied Shear Stress:
    \(R \approx y = 1\) m
    \[\tau_0 = 10{,}000 \times 1 \times S = 10{,}000 S \text{ N/m}^2\]
  2. Equate to Permissible Stress:
    \[10{,}000 S = 10 \implies S = \dfrac{1}{1000}\]
  3. Solve for \(n\):
    \[S = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1000} \implies n = 1000\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1000  |  Accepted key range: 1000 to 1000

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A bridge with an expected life of 50 years is designed for a flood of 10000 m³/s corresponding to the return period of 100 years. The risk associated with this design is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Flood Routing & Probability

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Expected life of bridge: \(n = 50\) years
    • Design flood discharge = 10,000 m³/s
    • Return period: \(T = 100\) years
  • Aim: Calculate the risk associated with this design.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Annual Probability of Exceedance: \(p = 1/T\)
  • Probability of Non-Exceedance: \(q = 1 - p\)
  • Risk: Probability that design flood is exceeded at least once during life \(n\):
    \[R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate probabilities:
    \(p = 1/100 = 0.01\), \(\quad q = 0.99\)
  2. Calculate Risk:
    \[R = 1 - (0.99)^{50} = 1 - 0.60501 = 0.39499\]
  3. Round to two decimal places:
    \(R \approx 0.39\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.39  |  Accepted key range: 0.38 to 0.41

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q56
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
An infinite slope with slope angle \( \beta = 22^\circ \) consists of soil with the following properties:
Unit weight \( \gamma = 15.72 \) kN/m³
Cohesion \( c' = 12 \) kPa
Angle of internal friction \( \phi' = 15^\circ \)
The critical height of the slope (in m) is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Stability of Slopes

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Slope angle: \(\beta = 22^\circ\)
    • Unit weight: \(\gamma = 15.72\) kN/m³
    • Cohesion: \(c' = 12\) kPa
    • Angle of internal friction: \(\phi' = 15^\circ\)
  • Aim: Find the critical height of the slope (\(H_c\)) in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Infinite Slope Stability (\(c\)-\(\phi\) soil):
    \[F_s = \dfrac{c' + \gamma z \cos^2\beta \tan\phi'}{\gamma z \cos\beta \sin\beta}\]
  • Critical Height: Set \(F_s = 1\) and \(z = H_c\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Rearrange for \(H_c\):
    \[\gamma H_c(\tan\beta - \tan\phi') = \dfrac{c'}{\cos^2\beta}\]
    \[H_c = \dfrac{c'}{\gamma \cos^2\beta (\tan\beta - \tan\phi')}\]
  2. Compute trigonometric values:
    \(\cos(22^\circ) = 0.92718 \implies \cos^2(22^\circ) = 0.85967\)
    \(\tan(22^\circ) = 0.40403\)
    \(\tan(15^\circ) = 0.26795\)
    \(\tan\beta - \tan\phi' = 0.40403 - 0.26795 = 0.13608\)
  3. Final Calculation:
    \[H_c = \dfrac{12}{15.72 \times 0.85967 \times 0.13608} = \dfrac{12}{1.8389} = 6.53 \text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 6.53 m  |  Accepted key range: 6.40 to 6.80

questions.question:
A circular pile of 600 mm diameter and 6 m length is embedded in a saturated clayey soil. Undrained cohesion of the soil is 80 kPa. Unit weight of the soil is 19.20 kN/m³. The adhesion factor is 0.54. If the diameter of the pile is doubled to 1200 mm (keeping the length constant), the ratio of pile capacity of 1200 mm diameter pile to that of 600 mm diameter pile is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations (Pile Capacity)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Pile 1: \(D_1 = 0.6\) m, \(L_1 = 6\) m
    • Pile 2: \(D_2 = 1.2\) m, \(L_2 = 6\) m
    • Undrained cohesion: \(c_u = 80\) kPa
    • Adhesion factor: \(\alpha = 0.54\)
  • Aim: Ratio of pile capacity of 1200 mm pile to 600 mm pile.

3. Core Concepts:

Ultimate Pile Capacity in Clay (\(\phi_u = 0\)):

\[Q_u = c_u N_c A_b + \alpha c_u A_s\]

where \(N_c = 9\) (Skempton's factor), \(A_b = \dfrac{\pi}{4}D^2\), \(A_s = \pi D L\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. General capacity equation:
    \[Q_u(D) = 9(80)\dfrac{\pi}{4}D^2 + 0.54(80)(\pi)(D)(6) = 180\pi D^2 + 259.2\pi D\]
  2. Pile 1 (\(D = 0.6\) m):
    \[Q_{u1} = 180\pi(0.36) + 259.2\pi(0.6) = 64.8\pi + 155.52\pi = 220.32\pi \text{ kN}\]
  3. Pile 2 (\(D = 1.2\) m):
    \[Q_{u2} = 180\pi(1.44) + 259.2\pi(1.2) = 259.2\pi + 311.04\pi = 570.24\pi \text{ kN}\]
  4. Ratio:
    \[\dfrac{Q_{u2}}{Q_{u1}} = \dfrac{570.24\pi}{220.32\pi} = 2.59\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.59  |  Accepted key range: 2.50 to 2.65

questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A group of 25 circular piles is arranged in 5 × 5 uniform pattern in a soft clay soil with equal spacing in both the directions. These are friction piles with negligible end bearing.

Consider the following details:
Diameter of each pile = 1 m
Length of each pile = 15 m
Cohesion of the soil = 20 kN/m²
Unit weight of the soil = 16 kN/m³
Adhesion factor = 0.75

Considering the efficiency of the pile group as unity, the optimum value of the ratio of the pile spacing to pile diameter is _______
(rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations (Pile Groups)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • 25 piles in a \(5 \times 5\) grid; \(D = 1\) m, \(L = 15\) m
    • Soil cohesion: \(c = 20\) kN/m²; Adhesion factor: \(\alpha = 0.75\)
    • Group efficiency: \(\eta = 1\)
    • Friction piles with negligible end bearing.
  • Aim: Find the optimum ratio of spacing to diameter (\(S/D\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Group Efficiency: \(\eta = 1 \implies Q_{ug} = n \cdot Q_u\)
  • Individual Pile Capacity (no end bearing): \(Q_u = \alpha c (\pi D L)\)
  • Block Failure Capacity (side friction only, block width \(B = 4S + D\) for \(5 \times 5\) group):
    \(Q_{ug} = c \times 4B \times L\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Individual Capacity:
    \[Q_u = 0.75 \times 20 \times \pi \times 1 \times 15 = 225\pi \text{ kN}\]
    \[\Sigma Q_u = 25 \times 225\pi = 5625\pi \approx 17{,}671.46 \text{ kN}\]
  2. Block Capacity Formulation:
    Block width: \(B = 4S + 1\)
    \[Q_{ug} = 20 \times 4B \times 15 = 1200B \text{ kN}\]
  3. Equate and Solve for \(B\):
    \[1200B = 17{,}671.46 \implies B = 14.726 \text{ m}\]
  4. Solve for \(S/D\):
    \[4S + 1 = 14.726 \implies S = 3.432 \text{ m}\]
    \[S/D = 3.432 / 1 = 3.43\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.4  |  Accepted key range: 3.2 to 3.6

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A shallow strip footing of width 2 m is embedded at a depth of 1.5 m below the ground surface in a homogeneous pure clay with an angle of internal friction zero. Consider unit weight of soil as 20 kN/m³ and undrained cohesion of soil as 20 kN/m².

Due to rise of ground water table from far below the founding depth to the ground surface in monsoon season, the magnitude of percentage change in the net ultimate bearing capacity as per Terzaghi’s theory is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shallow Foundations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Strip footing: \(B = 2\) m, \(D_f = 1.5\) m
    • Pure clay: \(\phi = 0\), \(c_u = 20\) kN/m²
    • Unit weight: \(\gamma = 20\) kN/m³
    • Initial state: Water table far below foundation.
    • Final state: Water table rises to ground surface.
  • Aim: Magnitude of percentage change in the net ultimate bearing capacity as per Terzaghi's theory.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Terzaghi's Ultimate Bearing Capacity:
    \[q_u = c_u N_c + \gamma_1 D_f N_q + 0.5\,\gamma_2\, B\, N_\gamma\]
  • For Pure Clay (\(\phi = 0\)): \(N_c = 5.7\), \(N_q = 1\), \(N_\gamma = 0\).
    \[q_u = c_u N_c + \gamma_1 D_f\]
  • Net Ultimate Bearing Capacity:
    \[q_{nu} = q_u - \gamma_1 D_f = c_u N_c\]
    This is completely independent of soil unit weight and water table position.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial Net Capacity:
    \[q_{nu(\text{initial})} = c_u \times N_c = 20 \times 5.7 = 114 \text{ kPa}\]
  2. Final Net Capacity (water table at surface):
    \[q_{nu(\text{final})} = c_u \times N_c = 20 \times 5.7 = 114 \text{ kPa}\]
    (The \(N_\gamma\) term is zero and the \(N_q\) surcharge cancels exactly in the net calculation.)
  3. Percentage Change:
    \[\% \text{ Change} = \dfrac{114 - 114}{114} \times 100 = 0\%\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.00%  |  Accepted key range: 0.00 to 0.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
Traffic is moving on a 6-lane dual carriageway road. Traffic volume per direction during peak hour (08:00 am to 09:00 am) is 6000 veh/h. It is assumed that the traffic is distributed uniformly across the lanes in each direction. Just at 08:00 am, a truck goes out of order on the middle lane of one side, thus disrupting the traffic on that lane in one direction. The lane capacity under normal conditions is 2000 veh/h/ln and under queue formation it is 1600 veh/h/ln. The traffic resumes at 08:30 am on removing the truck from the middle lane. Hourly traffic volume after 09:00 am reduces to 5000 veh/h/dir.

The number of vehicles in the queue at 10:00 am is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Traffic Engineering | Traffic Flow & Queuing Theory

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Road type: 6-lane dual carriageway (3 lanes per direction)
    • Peak demand: 6000 veh/h (08:00–09:00 AM), 5000 veh/h (after 09:00 AM)
    • Normal capacity: \(C_n = 2000\) veh/h/lane
    • Queue formation capacity: \(C_q = 1600\) veh/h/lane
    • Incident: Truck blocks middle lane from 08:00 to 08:30 AM (only 2 lanes open)
  • Aim: Calculate the total number of vehicles in the queue at 10:00 AM.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Queuing Theory: Queue forms whenever arrival rate (demand) exceeds departure rate (capacity).
  • Capacity Drop Phenomenon: Once a queue is established, discharge drops from free-flow capacity (2000 veh/h/lane) to queue-discharge capacity (1600 veh/h/lane).
  • Mass Balance Equation:
    \[Q_{t_2} = Q_{t_1} + (\text{Arrival Rate} - \text{Discharge Rate}) \times \Delta t\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Interval 1: 08:00–08:30 AM (\(\Delta t = 0.5\) h)
    Demand = 6000 veh/h; 2 lanes open.
    Free-flow capacity = \(2 \times 2000 = 4000\) veh/h < 6000 → queue forms.
    Discharge rate = \(2 \times 1600 = 3200\) veh/h.
    \[Q_1 = 0 + (6000 - 3200) \times 0.5 = 1400 \text{ veh}\]
  2. Interval 2: 08:30–09:00 AM (\(\Delta t = 0.5\) h)
    Demand = 6000 veh/h; 3 lanes open, but queue of 1400 veh still exists → discharge remains at queue capacity.
    Discharge rate = \(3 \times 1600 = 4800\) veh/h.
    \[Q_2 = 1400 + (6000 - 4800) \times 0.5 = 1400 + 600 = 2000 \text{ veh}\]
  3. Interval 3: 09:00–10:00 AM (\(\Delta t = 1.0\) h)
    New demand = 5000 veh/h; 3 lanes open. Since 5000 > 4800, queue continues to grow.
    Discharge rate = 4800 veh/h.
    \[Q_3 = 2000 + (5000 - 4800) \times 1.0 = 2000 + 200 = 2200 \text{ veh}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2200 vehicles  |  Accepted key range: 2200 to 2200

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
In a bituminous mix, the percentage by weight of coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, filler, and bituminous binder is 58, 25, 12, and 5, respectively. The corresponding specific gravity of these materials is 2.68, 2.45, 2.42, and 1.15. The bulk specific gravity of the mix is 2.2.

The Voids Filled with Bitumen (VFB, in percentage) is _______
(rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Highway Engineering | Pavement Materials (Bituminous Mix Design)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ComponentWeight % (\(W_i\))Specific Gravity (\(G_i\))
    Coarse Aggregate58%2.68
    Fine Aggregate25%2.45
    Filler12%2.42
    Bitumen Binder5%1.15
    Bulk specific gravity of mix: \(G_{mb} = 2.2\)
  • Aim: Find the Voids Filled with Bitumen (VFB) in %.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Theoretical Maximum Specific Gravity: \(G_{mm} = \dfrac{100}{\sum(W_i/G_i)}\)
  • Air Voids: \(V_a = \dfrac{G_{mm} - G_{mb}}{G_{mm}} \times 100\)
  • Volume of Bitumen: \(V_b = G_{mb} \times \dfrac{W_b}{G_b}\)
  • VMA and VFB: \(VMA = V_a + V_b\); \(\quad VFB = \dfrac{V_b}{VMA} \times 100\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate \(G_{mm}\):
    \[\sum\dfrac{W_i}{G_i} = \dfrac{58}{2.68} + \dfrac{25}{2.45} + \dfrac{12}{2.42} + \dfrac{5}{1.15} = 21.642 + 10.204 + 4.959 + 4.348 = 41.152\]
    \[G_{mm} = \dfrac{100}{41.152} = 2.430\]
  2. Calculate Air Voids (\(V_a\)):
    \[V_a = \dfrac{2.430 - 2.20}{2.430} \times 100 = 9.465\%\]
  3. Calculate Volume of Bitumen (\(V_b\)):
    \[V_b = 2.20 \times \dfrac{5}{1.15} = 9.565\%\]
  4. Calculate VMA and VFB:
    \[VMA = 9.465 + 9.565 = 19.030\%\]
    \[VFB = \dfrac{9.565}{19.030} \times 100 = 50.26\% \approx 50\%\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 50%  |  Accepted key range: 48 to 52

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q62
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
The following consecutive readings (in m) were taken with a dumpy level and a levelling staff at a common interval of 20 m:
0.385; 1.030; 1.925; 2.825; 3.730; 4.850; 1.045; 2.005; 3.330; 4.580

The dumpy level was shifted after taking the sixth reading.

The gradient (in %) of the ground between the first and the last location of the reading is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • 10 consecutive staff readings (m): 0.385, 1.030, 1.925, 2.825, 3.730, 4.850, 1.045, 2.005, 3.330, 4.580
    • Interval = 20 m; Instrument shifted after the 6th reading.
  • Aim: Calculate the ground gradient (%) between the first and last staff location.

3. Core Concepts:

  • First reading of each setup = Back Sight (BS); last reading before shifting = Fore Sight (FS); others = Intermediate Sights (IS).
  • Total Elevation Difference: \(\Delta H = \sum BS - \sum FS\)
  • Gradient (%): \(\left(\dfrac{\Delta H}{\text{Total Distance}}\right) \times 100\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Categorize readings:
    SetupReading No.TypeValue (m)
    Setup 11BS0.385
    2IS1.030
    3IS1.925
    4IS2.825
    5IS3.730
    6FS4.850
    Setup 27BS1.045
    8IS2.005
    9IS3.330
    10FS4.580
  2. Total Elevation Difference:
    \[\sum BS = 0.385 + 1.045 = 1.430 \text{ m}\]
    \[\sum FS = 4.850 + 4.580 = 9.430 \text{ m}\]
    \[\Delta H = 1.430 - 9.430 = -8.000 \text{ m}\]
    (Negative: last station is 8 m lower than first.)
  3. Horizontal Distance:
    Readings 6 and 7 are at the same station → total stations = 9 → intervals = 8.
    \(L = 8 \times 20 = 160\) m.
  4. Gradient:
    \[\text{Gradient} = \dfrac{-8.000}{160} \times 100 = -5\%\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: −5% (falling gradient of 5%)  |  Accepted key range: −5 to −5 (or 5 to 5)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q63
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
An Activated Sludge Process (ASP) has an inlet wastewater flowrate of 20000 m³/day with a Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) concentration of 250 mg/l. It produces treated wastewater containing 20 mg/l BOD. The aeration tank has a working volume of 6000 m³ and a biomass concentration of 3000 mg/l. Biological Sludge Residence Time (BSRT) of the system is 6 days. The influent wastewater and the treated effluent from the system have negligible concentrations of biomass. The sludge recycle line from the bottom of the Secondary Sedimentation Tank (SST) to the inlet of the aeration tank has a flowrate of 6000 m³/day.

To maintain equilibrium, the flowrate (in m³/day) of sludge that is to be wasted from the system is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment (Activated Sludge Process)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Influent flowrate: \(Q_0 = 20{,}000\) m³/day
    • Aeration tank volume: \(V = 6{,}000\) m³
    • MLSS concentration: \(X = 3{,}000\) mg/L
    • Mean cell residence time: \(\theta_c = 6\) days
    • Sludge recycle flowrate: \(Q_R = 6{,}000\) m³/day
    • Effluent biomass: \(X_e = 0\) mg/L (negligible)
  • Aim: Determine the flowrate of sludge wasted (\(Q_w\)) in m³/day.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Biological Sludge Residence Time (BSRT):
    \[\theta_c = \dfrac{V \cdot X}{Q_w \cdot X_u} \quad (\text{with } X_e = 0)\]
  • Mass Balance at SST (to find underflow concentration \(X_u\)):
    \[X_u = \dfrac{(Q_0 + Q_R) \cdot X}{Q_R + Q_w}\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Substitute \(X_u\) into \(\theta_c\) equation:
    \[\theta_c = \dfrac{V \cdot (Q_R + Q_w)}{Q_w \cdot (Q_0 + Q_R)}\]
    (MLSS \(X\) cancels out.)
  2. Plug in values:
    \[6 = \dfrac{6000(6000 + Q_w)}{Q_w \times 26000}\]
  3. Solve for \(Q_w\):
    \[6 \times 26000 \times Q_w = 6000(6000 + Q_w)\]
    Divide both sides by 6000:
    \[26 Q_w = 6000 + Q_w\]
    \[25 Q_w = 6000 \implies Q_w = 240 \text{ m}^3/\text{day}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 240 m³/day  |  Accepted key range: 230 to 250

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
The intensity-duration relationship for a rainfall on a rectangular plot ABCD of area 7 ha (1 ha = 10⁴ m²) can be modelled by the following equation:
\[I = \dfrac{25}{(t + 10)} \]
where \( I \) is rainfall intensity (in cm/h), and \( t \) is the duration (in minutes) of rainfall. The average runoff coefficient over the area is 0.60. The time of entry (in minutes) to the outfall from the corners A, B, C, and D is 10, 20, 15 and 25, respectively.

The design flowrate (in m³/h) of the storm-sewer at the outfall is _______
(in integer).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Surface Water Runoff (Rational Method)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area: \(A = 7\) ha \(= 7 \times 10^4\) m²
    • Runoff coefficient: \(C = 0.60\)
    • Rainfall intensity: \(I = \dfrac{25}{t+10}\) cm/h (\(t\) in min)
    • Time of entry from corners A, B, C, D: 10, 20, 15, 25 min
  • Aim: Calculate the design peak flowrate (\(Q\)) in m³/h.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Rational Formula: \(Q = C \cdot I \cdot A\)
  • Time of Concentration (\(t_c\)): Time for water to travel from the hydraulically most remote point to the outfall — ensures entire catchment contributes to peak:
    \[t_c = \max(t_{\text{entry}})\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Time of Concentration:
    \[t_c = \max(10, 20, 15, 25) = 25 \text{ min}\]
  2. Critical Rainfall Intensity:
    \[I = \dfrac{25}{25 + 10} = \dfrac{25}{35} = \dfrac{5}{7} \text{ cm/h} = \dfrac{5}{7} \times 10^{-2} \text{ m/h}\]
  3. Design Flowrate:
    \[Q = 0.60 \times \dfrac{5}{7} \times 10^{-2} \times 7 \times 10^4\]
    \[Q = 0.60 \times \dfrac{5}{7} \times 700 = 0.60 \times 500 = 300 \text{ m}^3/\text{h}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 300 m³/h  |  Accepted key range: 300 to 300

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q65
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The maximum demand at a water purification plant has been estimated as 12 million litres per day. For the raw supplies, a rectangular sedimentation tank is to be designed with mechanical sludge removal arrangement. Consider depth of the tank as 4 m, detention period as 6 hours, and velocity of flow as 0.003 m/s.

The width (in m) of the detention tank is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Sedimentation Tank)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Design flow: \(Q = 12\) MLD
    • Tank depth: \(H = 4\) m
    • Detention period: \(t_d = 6\) hours
    • Flow velocity: \(V_f = 0.003\) m/s
  • Aim: Determine the width (\(W\)) of the rectangular sedimentation tank in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity Equation: \(Q = A_c \times V_f \implies A_c = Q/V_f\)
  • Geometric Relation: \(A_c = W \times H\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert \(Q\) to m³/s:
    \(Q = 12{,}000 \text{ m}^3/\text{day} = \dfrac{12{,}000}{86{,}400} = 0.13889 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
  2. Calculate Cross-Sectional Area:
    \[A_c = \dfrac{0.13889}{0.003} = 46.296 \text{ m}^2\]
  3. Calculate Width:
    \[W = \dfrac{A_c}{H} = \dfrac{46.296}{4} = 11.574 \approx 11.57 \text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 11.57 m  |  Accepted key range: 11.00 to 12.00
